part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who makes up the College of the European Commission?

options.A: The EU Commission President and the High Representative for Foreign Affairs
options.B: The President of the Commission, plus eight Vice-Presidents
options.C: One Commissioner per member state (27 Commissioners), led by the Commission President
options.D: A team of 20 Commissioners with independent decision-making powers

rationale: The European Commission is led by a College of 27 Commissioners (one from each EU country, including the Commission President). The Commission President decides which Commissioner is responsible for each policy area. Decisions are taken based on collective responsibility, so all Commissioners are equal in deciding and being accountable for the College’s decisions. They generally do not have any individual decision-making powers. Reference: https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/institutions-andbodies/institutions-and-bodies-profiles/european-commission_en#:~:text=The%20College%20of%20Commissioners %20is,each%20responsible%20for%20a%20portfolio.

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Which of these are competencies of the EU Commission?

options.A: Manages EU policies and allocates EU funding
options.B: Adopts and amends legislative proposals
options.C: Decides on the EU's foreign and security policies
options.D: Decides on the political direction of the EU and adopts the EU budget

rationale: The Commission helps to shape the EU's strategy, proposes new EU legislation and policies, monitors their implementation and manages the EU budget. Legislation is adopted and amended by the EU Parliament and the Council of the EU. The broad parameters of political direction and foreign policy are to a large degree set by the European Council and implemented by the Council and Commission. Reference: https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/institutions-and-bodies/institutions-and-bodies-profiles /european-commission_en#:~:text=The%20College%20of%20Commissioners%20is,each%20responsible %20for%20a%20portfolio.

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Which of the following is the EU’s independent executive arm?

options.B: The European Parliament
options.C: The Council of the EU
options.D: The European Commission

rationale: The European Commission is the EU's politically independent executive arm. It alone is responsible for drawing up proposals for new European legislation, and it implements the decisions of the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. Reference: https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-lawbudget/institutions-and-bodies/institutions-and-bodies-profiles/european-commission_en#:~:text=The%20College %20of%20Commissioners%20is,each%20responsible%20for%20a%20portfolio.

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who decides on the European Commission’s internal organisation and assigns portfolios to Commissioners?

options.A: The European Parliament President
options.B: Member States
options.C: The EU Commission President
options.D: The President of the Council

rationale: The President of the Commission sets out the political guidelines for the Commission, decides on its internal organisation and assigns portfolios to the Commissioners. The responsibilities of individual Commissioners may change during the course of the Commission’s mandate (5 years). Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/rules-of-procedure-of-the-european-commission.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: According to the EU Commission’s rules of procedure, which of the following are the types of internal decision-making procedures?

options.A: Oral, written, empowerment, and delegation procedures
options.B: Delegation and implementation procedures
options.C: Regular and exceptional procedures
options.D: Oral and written procedures, and special case procedures

rationale: There are 4 types of internal decision-making procedures in the EU Commission: – Oral procedure: the Commission takes decisions (such as political or economic decisions) during its ordinary or extraordinary meetings via this procedure. – Written procedure: these are adopted when Commissioners do not express reservations or request changes to a draft proposal within a specific time limit. – Empowerment procedure: the Commission empowers one or several members of the Commission to manage a situation on its behalf. – Delegation procedure: the Commission delegates the power to adopt certain measures to directorsgeneral or heads of service of behalf of the Institution. Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legalcontent/summary/rules-of-procedure-of-the-european-commission.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What was the effect of the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the EU on the number of seats in the EU Parliament?

options.A: There was no change, there are still currently 750 seats
options.B: The UK’s 73 seats were redistributed evenly amongst member states, maintaining the total of 750 seats
options.C: The total seats were decreased to 705, with some member states gaining seats
options.D: The 73 British MEPs’ seats were eliminated, leaving 677 seats in total

rationale: The total number of parliamentary seats was reduced from 751 to 705. As this reduction in total was less than the 73 seats that had been held by the UK, it meant that some Member States saw their number of seats increased. Reference: https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/20/the-european-parliament-organisation-and-operation

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: How is the number of MEPs per member state calculated?

options.A: By degressive proportionality: no country can have fewer than 6 or more than 96 MEPs
options.B: It is a first-past-the-post electoral system (FPTP or FPP)
options.C: It depends on the European election results in each Member State, and small countries always have 5 MEPs to ensure representation
options.D: Proportionally to the country’s population size, plus one MEP for large countries

rationale: The number of MEPs for each member states is to some degree proportionate to its population, but degressive proportionality is used: no country can have fewer than 6 or more than 96 MEPs; and the total number of MEPs cannot exceed 705 (704 plus the President), a number which changed following Brexit (previously 750 MEPs). This system means that, to ensure they have an adequate voice, less populous countries are over-represented, in strictly proportional terms, compared with the countries with larger populations. Reference: https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/20/the-european-parliament-organisation-and-operation

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Where is the official seat of the EU Parliament?

options.A: Strasbourg, Brussels and Luxembourg jointly
options.B: Strasbourg
options.C: Brussels
options.D: There is no official seat

rationale: The European Council confirmed in 1992 (what was already by then the practical reality) that the European Parliament has three principal places of work: Strasbourg (its official seat), Brussels and Luxembourg. In 1997 the arrangement was incorporated into the EU treaty. Reference: https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/faq/18/why-does-parliament-move-between-brussels-and-strasbourg

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Members of the European Parliament sit in the chamber according to:

rationale: The Conference of Presidents of the European Parliament decides how MEPs will sit at the start of each legislative term. Over the past terms, political groups, made up of loosely affiliated similar political parties from different member states, have been put together like wedges in a pie chart. Reference: https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/faq/2/seating-in-the-chamber

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union

The President represents the European Parliament to the outside world and also in its relations with the other EU institutions. Reference: https://the-president.europarl.europa.eu/en/thepresidency/functions

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: How are the main EU competences divided?

options.A: They are binding and non-binding
options.B: They are regular or special
options.C: This depends on the principle of subsidiarity
options.D: They are exclusive, shared or supporting

rationale: The Treaty of Lisbon defines the division of competences between the EU and its member states. These competences are divided into three main categories: – exclusive competences of the EU (the EU alone can legislate) – shared competences (the EU and member states legislate) – supporting competences (the EU can only intervene to support member states) Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/division-of-competences-within-the-europeanunion.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Which institution adopts the final decision to conclude international agreements?

options.A: It depends on the agreement - for trade it is the Commission, for others it is the Council
options.B: The European Commission
options.C: The Council
options.D: The EU Parliament

rationale: The Council adopts the final decision to conclude agreements (negotiated on behalf of the EU by the Commission) between the EU and non-EU countries and international organisations, once the Parliament has given its consent, and it has been ratified by all EU member states. Reference: https://www.consilium. europa.eu/en/council-eu/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who attends COREPER II meetings?

options.A: Permanent representatives of the member states who deal with Employment, Social Policy, Health and Consumer Affairs; Competitiveness (Internal Market, Industry, Research and Space); and Foreign Affairs
options.B: Permanent representatives of the Member States, who deal with General Foreign Affairs, Economic and Financial, and Justice and Home Affairs configurations of the Council
options.C: Deputy permanent representatives, preparing all Council configurations
options.D: Permanent representatives, MEPs and civil society representatives

rationale: The work of the Council is prepared by the Committee of Permanent Representatives of the Member States (Coreper). Coreper is divided into: – Coreper II, composed of the permanent representatives of the governments of the Member States, deals with items relating to the General Affairs, Foreign Affairs, Economic and Financial Affairs and Justice and Home Affairs configurations of the Council – Coreper I, composed of the deputy permanent representatives, prepares all other Council configurations. Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/council-of-the-european-union.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who can chair COREPER meetings?

options.A: They are always chaired by the delegate of the country holding the rotating 6-month presidency of the Council of the EU
options.B: They are chaired by the president of the Council of the EU
options.C: An appointed specialist who heads the working party
options.D: They can be chaired by an elected chairperson, the rotating 6-month presidency representative, by a representative of the High Representative, or others

rationale: These meetings can be chaired by an appointed or elected chairperson, the delegate of the country holding the rotating 6-month presidency of the Council, by a representative of the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy or by the General Secretariat of the Council. Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/council-preparatory-bodies.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who are members of the European Council?

options.A: EU heads of state, exclusively
options.B: EU heads of state or government, and the Presidents of the European Council and the Commission
options.C: EU heads of state or government, and the Presidents of all the other EU institutions
options.D: EU heads of government, and external guests invited to their meetings

rationale: The members of the European Council are the heads of state or government of the 27 EU member states, the European Council President and the President of the European Commission. Reference: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/european-council/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is the purpose of the Court of Justice of the EU?

options.A: To provide a forum for judges from the 27 member states to formulate uniform legal standards in the member states
options.B: To act as guardian of the EU Treaties
options.C: To support its 3 principal judges in deciding on cases brought before the Court
options.D: To ensure the uniform interpretation of EU law and that EU countries and institutions respect the law

rationale: The purpose of the Court of Justice of the European Union is to ensure the uniform interpretation of EU law and that EU countries and institutions respect the law. The Court is composed of 27 judges (1 from each EU country) and 11 advocates-general, who present opinions on cases brought before the Court. They are appointed by common accord of EU countries for 6 years. (It is the European Commission that has the role of guardian of the treaties.) Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/court-ofjustice.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What are the two main branches of the CJEU?

options.A: The Court of Justice and the General Court
options.B: The Court of Auditors and the General Court
options.C: The Court of EU judges and the Specialised Court
options.D: The Specialised Court and the General Court

rationale: The CJEU has 2 branches: – – The Court of Justice: mainly gives preliminary rulings, hears some actions against EU institutions brought by EU countries and takes appeals from the General Court. The General Court: has jurisdiction to hear actions against EU institutions brought by citizens and, in some instances, other EU countries. Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legalcontent/glossary/court-of-justice-of-the-european-union.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: The Court of Justice of the EU is responsible for dealing with:

options.A: Actions brought by an EU country or the Commission against an EU country for infringing EU law
options.B: Individual or State applications of violations of the civil rights set out in the European Convention on Human Rights
options.C: Securing the right to life, respect for private life, and freedom of expression
options.D: Applying EU law to a dispute brought by a referring court

rationale: The Court is responsible for dealing with: – references for preliminary rulings from national courts on interpretation of EU law – actions brought by an EU country or the Commission against an EU country for infringing EU law – some actions brought by an EU country for annulment of a measure adopted by an EU institution – actions against an EU institution for failure to act – appeals on points of law against judgments of the General Court The CJEU does not apply EU law to a dispute brought by a referring court. Its role is only to help resolve these. It is the (non-EU) European Court of Human Rights that has jurisdiction in respect of the European Convention on Human Rights, to which non-EU states are also parties. Reference: https://eurlex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/court-of-justice.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is the composition of the CJEU?

options.A: 28 Judges and 28 Counsels
options.B: 27 Judges
options.C: 27 Judges and 11 Advocates General
options.D: It varies based on the case in question

rationale: The Court of Justice is composed of 27 Judges and 11 Advocates General. The Judges and Advocates General are appointed by agreement of the governments of the Member States after consultation of a responsible panel. They are appointed for a renewable term of six years. Reference: https://curia.europa.eu/jcms/jcms/Jo2_7024/en/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: According to the fundamental principles laid down in Article 5 of the TEU, what does proportionality mean?

options.A: That the EU can only act in so far as member states have given it the power to do so
options.B: That for non-exclusive competences, the EU may act only if – and in so far as – the objective of a proposed action cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States, but could be better achieved at EU level
options.C: That the content and scope of EU action may not go beyond what is necessary to achieve the objectives of the treaties
options.D: That the EU must always act proportionally to the issue at stake

rationale: As set out in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union: – Proportionality: The content and scope of EU action may not go beyond what is necessary to achieve the objectives of the treaties. – Subsidiarity: In the area of its non-exclusive competences, the EU may act only if – and in so far as – the objective of a proposed action cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States but could be better achieved at EU level. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/division-of-competenceswithin-the-european-union.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is a pre-condition for the Council to be able to vote?

options.A: Member states must be represented by a State Secretary
options.B: The chair must be the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
options.C: A majority of its members must be present
options.D: The voting must be unanimous

rationale: Council meetings are attended by representatives from each member state at a ministerial level. Participants can therefore be ministers or state secretaries. They have the right to commit the government of their country and cast its vote. European Commissioners responsible for the areas concerned are also invited to Council meetings. The Council can only vote if a majority of its members is present. Reference: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/council-eu/configurations/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is a Council configuration?

options.A: It is a type of meeting which is open to the public
options.B: A cross-sector grouping of ministers who meet informally to discuss overlapping issues such as health and employment
options.C: It is each of the technical formations of ministers, of which there are 10 in total
options.D: It is a hierarchical system of Council formations which take individual decisions in the name of the Council

rationale: The Council of the EU is a single legal entity, but it meets in 10 different “configurations”, depending on the subject being discussed. There is no hierarchy among the Council configurations, although the General Affairs Council and the Foreign Affairs Council have special roles. Reference: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/council-eu/configurations/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: How are EU agencies grouped?

options.A: Technical and scientific agencies, managerial agencies and Europol
options.B: Decentralised agencies, executive agencies, EURATOM and EIT
options.C: Technical agencies, EURATOM and EESC and Committee of the Regions
options.D: Technical and scientific agencies, EESC and Committee of the Regions

rationale: EU agencies are set up by the EU to carry out specific technical, scientific or administrative tasks. They are divided into 4 groups: – Decentralised agencies – Executive agencies – European Atomic Energy Community Treaty (EURATOM) agencies – European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT). Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legalcontent/glossary/european-union-agencies.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is Europol?

options.A: The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation, based in The Hague
options.B: The European Police Office and Drugs Unit, based in Lyon
options.C: The International Criminal Police Organization, based in Vienna
options.D: The European Police Border and Coast Guard Agency, based in Warsaw

rationale: Europol is an EU agency that seeks to assist member state (and other) police authorities and law enforcement services in preventing and combatting international organised crime and terrorism. It was established in The Hague in 1999, became a full EU agency in 2010 and given wider powers and its present name in 2017. Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/europol-european-union-agency-forlaw-enforcement-cooperation.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is the role of EFSA?

options.A: It is a part of the European Commission which provides advice on consumer protection in relation to food products
options.B: It is a decentralised agency which provides scientific advice on food safety to the EU and member states
options.C: It is an agency with the aim of encouraging healthy eating by EU consumers
options.D: It is an agency with the power to control which food products go on the market in the EU

rationale: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), in Parma, Italy, is an EU decentralised agency that provides independent scientific advice on food-related risks. This advice informs European laws and rules, and therefore helps protect consumers. Its remit covers: – food and feed safety – nutrition – animal health and welfare – plant protection – plant health. Reference: https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/institutions-and-bodies/institutions-andbodies-profiles/efsa_en

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What does EIGE stand for when talking about EU agencies?

options.A: European Innovation Governmental Entity
options.B: Economic and Investment Generation
options.C: European Initiative for Geothermal Energy
options.D: European Institute for Gender Equality

rationale: The European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) is an EU decentralised agency which supports efforts to bring about gender equality in the EU. It is based in Vilnius (Lithuania). Reference: https://eige.europa.eu/

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: Who has responsibility for control of the EU’s external borders?

options.A: Frontex
options.B: Individual member states with an external border
options.C: The EU Commission
options.D: It is a shared responsibility of the Commission and the member states

rationale: Member states that have an external border have total responsibility for border control. However, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) increasingly provides additional practical support for EU countries in managing the EU’s external borders in respect of challenges such as cross-border crime and migratory pressures. Reference: https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/institutions-andbodies/institutions-and-bodies-profiles/frontex_en

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: What is the European Banking Authority (EBA)?

options.A: A department within the European Central Bank which aims to create Single Rulebook in banking
options.B: An independent agency for regulation and supervision of the EU banking sector
options.C: A subsection of the Committee of European Banking Supervisors
options.D: A European system for financial supervision run by the European Systemic Risk Board

rationale: The European Banking Authority (EBA) is an independent EU authority based in Paris which works to ensure effective and consistent regulation and supervision across the EU banking sector. Its overall aims are to maintain financial stability in the EU and to safeguard the orderly functioning of the banking sector. It is one of the mechanisms set up in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crash. Reference: https://eurlex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/european-banking-authority-eba.html

part: II. Institutions, other bodies and agencies of the European Union
prompt: HERA (Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority), created in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, is:

options.A: An EU Executive Agency
options.B: A new European Commission Directorate- General
options.C: An independent body, similar to the EEAS
options.D: An EU decentralised agency

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU
prompt: Which of the following make up EU primary law?

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU
prompt: Which statement is true about EU regulations?

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU
prompt: What is the process of transposition?

options.B: It is a necessary process for EU regulations and decisions, since they are not directly applicable

rationale: Transposition is the process according to which member states incorporate EU directives into their national laws. It applies to directives, since they are not directly applicable in member states, unlike regulations and decisions. The EU member states must adopt these national laws within a deadline, set out in the directive, and must notify their implementing measures to the European Commission. If the member state does not adopt said national laws, or if the measures are unsatisfactory, the Commission may take a case to the Court of Justice of the European Union. Reference: EUR-Lex - transposition - EN - EUR-Lex (europa.eu)

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU
prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic of Delegated Acts?

Reference: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/delegated-acts.html

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU

part: III. Legislative procedures of the EU
